I am submitting this complaint based on new and continuing servicing conduct that occurred through Aidvantages XX/XX/XXXXXXXX final response to CFPB Complaint # XXXX. This complaint is not merely a repetition of my earlier complaint concerning the resumption of interest in XX/XX/XXXX. It concerns Aidvantages subsequent failure to answer a direct servicing question, failure to provide specifically requested account records, and continued collection and application of substantial payments without providing an adequate individualized accounting. My prior complaint expressly asked Aidvantage to answer whether Aidvantage itself sent me account-level notice that interest would begin accruing again on or around XX/XX/XXXXXXXX while my loans remained in SAVE-related forbearance. Aidvantages XX/XX/XXXX response did not answer yes or no. Instead, Aidvantage stated that Federal Student Aid allegedly sent a general email to affected borrowers and directed me to contact FSA. That response avoids the actual question. Aidvantage did not state that it sent me notice. It did not state that it did not send me notice. It did not identify any Aidvantage email, letter, account alert, portal message, telephone communication, or other borrower-facing notice concerning the interest-rate change. Aidvantage also failed to produce the documentation specifically requested in my complaint. It did not provide : 1. A copy of the alleged FSA email or any record demonstrating that it was sent to me. 2. The date, recipient address, transmission record, delivery status, or message identifier for the alleged notice. 3. A loan-by-loan accounting of interest accrued after XX/XX/XXXX. 4. A payment application history showing how my payments were divided between interest and principal. 5. A reconciliation of Aidvantages XX/XX/XXXXXXXX written representation that my interest rate would remain at 0.00 % and that interest would not accrue during the forbearance. 6. The contractual, regulatory, or servicing basis for Aidvantages position that it had no obligation to provide any account-level communication concerning this material change. Aidvantage therefore treated a general statement about an alleged third-party email as a substitute for answering an individualized servicing inquiry and producing records concerning my own account. Directing me to FSA does not explain what Aidvantage did, what records Aidvantage possesses, how Aidvantage implemented the interest change, or how Aidvantage applied my payments after the change. This failure is especially material because Aidvantage continues to service my loans, calculate and display my balances, assess interest, accept payments, and determine how those payments are applied. Over the past 12 months, I have paid more than {$20000.00} toward these loans in good faith. Aidvantage has continued accepting and applying those funds while failing to provide the requested accounting and while refusing to answer a basic question about its own borrower-facing communications. I am not refusing repayment and I am not seeking to avoid my financial obligations. My substantial payment history demonstrates the opposite. However, a borrower who has paid more than {$20000.00} in XXXX year should be able to obtain a clear explanation of how those payments were applied, how much interest accrued, what notice was provided, and how the servicer reconciles its current position with its previous written representations. The new issue is therefore Aidvantages ongoing failure to provide adequate account-level service and records after receiving a formal CFPB complaint specifically requesting that information. A nearly 60-day investigation followed by a generic referral to FSA is not a substantive response to an audit request. Aidvantages response left every material accounting question unanswered while the company continued collecting payments and assessing interest.

Our travel agency became the victim of a payment fraud scheme involving international airline ticket purchases. Customers contacted our agency directly by telephone and XXXX to purchase airline tickets. Before issuing the tickets, we followed our standard verification procedures, including obtaining copies of the passenger 's passport and the credit card used for payment, maintaining direct telephone communication with the customer, and keeping complete booking and payment records. The payment transactions were successfully authorized by the issuing banks. In several cases, the transactions were approved without requiring XXXX Secure authentication. Based on the bank 's authorization and our own verification procedures, we had no reason to suspect fraud. The airline tickets were issued, and the passengers completed their travel. Airline records confirm that the flights were flown and that the services were fully provided. Only after the travel had been completed did the cardholders dispute the transactions as unauthorized. As a result, our agency has suffered financial losses totaling {$19000.00} through chargebacks, despite having delivered the purchased services in full. We have submitted evidence in the chargeback disputes, including passenger identification documents, booking records, payment information, customer communications, and flight records confirming that the transportation services were used. We also reported this matter to the Internet Crime Complaint Center ( XXXX ) on XX/XX/year>, and to our local police department. Unfortunately, local law enforcement advised that they were unable to investigate or provide further assistance. Complaint Against Goldman Sachs Bank USA Regarding Apple Card Monthly Installments, Misleading Balance Presentation, Credit Reporting Harm, and Refusal to Provide a Timely Remedy I am submitting this complaint against Goldman Sachs Bank USA, the issuer and credit-reporting furnisher for Apple Card, regarding the way Apple Card Monthly Installments are presented to consumers, reflected within the Apple Wallet interface, and subsequently reported to the consumer reporting agencies. This complaint is not based on a missed payment, delinquency, default, or failure to satisfy an account obligation. I have never been late on this account. My concern is that Goldman Sachs and Apple present Apple Card Monthly Installments as a low monthly payment arrangement while failing to prominently and meaningfully disclose that the entire remaining financed principal may be reported as revolving credit-card utilization, even though that full amount is not clearly reflected as the consumers current card balance or current payment obligation within the primary account display. This design is misleading, creates a foreseeable risk of substantial credit harm, and prevents consumers from making a fully informed decision about the financing product. Transaction and account history In XX/XX/year>, I purchased a MacBook Neo from Apple for approximately {$490.00} plus applicable sales tax. I specifically selected Apple Card Monthly Installments because the transaction was presented as an interest-free installment arrangement with a monthly payment of approximately {$41.00}. The Apple Card statement and primary account information presented the amount associated with the installment plan as a monthly obligation of {$41.00}. The full remaining installment principal was maintained separately within the Monthly Installments section rather than being clearly incorporated into the primary current card balance or payment amount displayed to me. Based on how the transaction and account balance were presented, I reasonably understood that the monthly installment would be the amount reflected as the current obligation associated with the financing arrangement. I was not provided with a sufficiently prominent warning at checkout, within the Wallet interface, or before the transaction was completed stating that : 1. The entire remaining financed balance would be reported to the credit bureaus as revolving credit-card utilization. 2. The amount reported to the credit bureaus could be substantially higher than the balance prominently displayed as currently due. 3. The resulting utilization increase could cause an immediate and significant credit-score reduction. XXXX. This could occur even when the account was fully current, the purchase was placed on a 0 % installment plan, and only a small monthly payment was due. On XX/XX/year>, Goldman Sachs reported an ending Apple Card balance of {$760.00} to XXXX That reported amount included the remaining financed purchase amount and other account activity, even though my statement reflected only the {$41.00} installment as the current installment payment. XXXX subsequently notified me that my credit score had decreased by XXXX points because of the reported increase in utilization. Immediate and serious mortgage-related harm This occurred while I was actively undergoing mortgage underwriting for the purchase of a home. Consumers are repeatedly instructed during the mortgage process not to open new accounts, incur substantial new debt, or materially increase credit-card balances. I intentionally selected the installment option because it was presented as a fixed monthly payment arrangement, and I believed that the credit impact would correspond to the stated monthly obligation. Instead, Goldman Sachs reported the full remaining financed amount as part of my revolving Apple Card balance without providing a prominent and understandable disclosure that this would occur. A XXXX credit-score decrease during active mortgage underwriting can affect : * Mortgage eligibility * Interest-rate qualification * Lender credits * Mortgage insurance * Debt and credit review requirements * Final underwriting approval * Closing conditions * The overall cost of borrowing The harm is not theoretical. I was required to notify my mortgage lender immediately and explain why my reported balance and credit score had unexpectedly changed during underwriting. I now face the possibility that the lender may require additional documentation, a credit supplement, a rapid rescore, or another credit review. I immediately paid the account in full As soon as I learned that Goldman Sachs had reported the full financed balance and that my score had decreased, I took immediate action. I paid the entire Apple Card balance in full, including : * The regular Apple Card balance * The remaining balance of the XXXX installment plan * Any other amount due on the account My Apple Card balance is now {$0.00}, and Apple has provided written confirmation showing that the current balance is {$0.00}. This was not a situation involving an inability or unwillingness to pay. Had the Apple Card interface clearly shown that the full installment principal would be reported as revolving utilization, or had it displayed the amount being furnished to the credit bureaus as the primary current card balance, I could have promptly paid the amount before the XX/XX/XXXX reporting date and avoided the damage. Instead, the product separated the amount currently presented as due from the much larger amount being treated as credit utilization for reporting purposes. Goldman Sachs refused to provide a meaningful remedy I contacted Goldman Sachs and opened case number XXXX to request assistance. I explained that : * The account was never delinquent. * The transaction was specifically placed on Apple Card Monthly Installments. * The statement reflected an installment payment of approximately {$41.00}. * Goldman Sachs reported a total balance of {$760.00}. * The reporting caused a XXXXXXXX XXXX score decrease. * I was actively undergoing mortgage underwriting. * I immediately paid the complete account and installment balance. * The current Apple Card balance is confirmed as {$0.00}. I requested that Goldman Sachs make a goodwill adjustment, provide an expedited or off-cycle update, or take another reasonable action to address the damage caused by this situation. Goldman Sachs representatives informed me that the company could not or would not make a goodwill adjustment or otherwise correct the reported balance before its normal reporting process. This response is inadequate. Goldman Sachs has been provided with documentation showing that the account is now paid in full and that the reported balance created an immediate risk to an active mortgage transaction. Nevertheless, Goldman Sachs has refused to provide a timely remedy or meaningful escalation. Telling a consumer to wait for a future reporting cycle is not a reasonable response when the financial harm is occurring now and may affect a time-sensitive mortgage approval. Deceptive and predatory effect of the installment structure I believe this practice is deceptive and predatory in effect. The product is marketed and presented around an affordable monthly installment. The consumer is shown the monthly amount due and is encouraged to view the transaction as a manageable, interest-free monthly obligation. However, the credit-reporting consequences are based on the entire remaining financed principal being treated as revolving credit utilization. The most important consequence of the financing arrangement is therefore not presented with the same prominence as the monthly payment being used to market the product. The consumer sees one amount as the current monthly obligation, while Goldman Sachs reports a substantially larger amount to the credit bureaus. That creates a material information imbalance. A reasonable consumer may believe that selecting a monthly installment option will result in the monthly installment being treated as the relevant monthly credit obligation. A consumer should not be expected to understand, without a prominent and specific disclosure, that the entire remaining financed amount will be reported as revolving utilization and could immediately reduce their credit score. The fact that the remaining installment principal may be located within a separate area of the Wallet application does not cure the problem. The interface should clearly display : * The amount currently due * The total remaining installment principal * The amount that may be reported as the credit-card balance * The effect the transaction may have on available credit and utilization * A clear warning that the full remaining amount may affect the consumers credit score This information should be presented before the consumer confirms the transaction, not discovered after the credit damage has occurred. Technical accuracy does not resolve the consumer-protection concern Goldman Sachs may respond that the reported amount was technically accurate because the remaining installment principal was owed under the Apple Card agreement. That response would not address the substance of this complaint. M y complaint concerns the material difference between : 1. How the product is marketed and presented to the consumer. 2. How the balance is displayed in the primary account interface. 3. What the consumer is told is currently due. 4. What Goldman Sachs reports as revolving credit utilization. 5. The absence of a clear warning about the foreseeable credit consequences. 6. Goldman Sachss refusal to provide an expedited remedy after the balance was paid in full. A practice may still be misleading or unfair when technically accurate information is presented in a manner that obscures a material consequence of the transaction. Consumers should not have to suffer a substantial credit-score reduction before learning how Goldman Sa chs reports Apple Card Monthly Installments. Requested investigation and resolution I request that the CFPB forward this complaint to Goldman Sachs Bank USA and require a substantive response addressing each issue raised. I specifically request that Goldman Sachs : 1. Conduct a formal investigation into the XX/XX/year> reporting of the {$760.00} balance. XXXX. Provide a detailed written breakdown of every amount included in the {$760.00} reported balance. XXXX. Identify the exact date the balance was furnished to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX 4. Explain whether the entire remaining Apple Card Monthly Installment principal is reported as revolving credit utilization. 5. Identify the specific disclosure presented to me before checkout that clearly stated the full remaining financed amount would be reported as revolving utilization and could negatively affect my credit score. 6. Provide a copy of the version of that disclosure that was in effect on the purchase date. 7. Explain why the full amount being furnished to the credit bureaus was not displayed as the primary current Apple Card balance available for immediate payment before the reporting date. 8. Submit an immediate off-cycle update to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX confirming that the account and installment balance are {$0.00}. 9. Where legally and operationally permissible, withdraw, revise, or otherwise correct the XX/XX/XXXX reporting so that the temporary installment balance does not continue to cause an inaccurate or misleading representation of my current credit utilization. 10. Provide written confirmation that the account was never delinquent, that no payment was missed, that the installment agreement was paid in full, and that the current account balance is {$0.00}. I need this documentation for my mortgage lender. 11. Confirm that no adverse, derogatory, disputed, or special comment code will be placed on the account in a manner that could create additional mortgage underwriting issues. 12. Review whether the Apple Card checkout process and Wallet interface clearly and conspicuously disclose the credit-reporting treatment of Monthly Installments. 13. Add a prominent pre-purchase warning advising consumers that the entire remaining financed amount may be reported as revolving credit utilization and may negatively affect their credit score. 14. Compensate me for any documented financial loss caused by this reporting, including increased mortgage pricing, lost lender credits, rapid-rescore expenses, delayed closing costs, or other direct damages. I am attaching or can provide the following supporting documentation : * Apple Card statement showing the {$41.00} installment * Apple Card Monthly Installment details * XXXX notification documenting the XXXX score decrease * Credit-report information showing the {$760.00} reported balance * Confirmation that the Apple Card balance is now {$0.00} * Confirmation that the installment plan was paid in full * Payment confirmation and bank records * Communications with Goldman Sachs * Goldman Sachs case information * Communications with my mortgage lender * Documentation of any resulting mortgage or financial impact I request a complete response rather than a generic statement that the information was reported accurately or that Goldman Sachs does not make goodwill adjustments. Goldman Sachs must address why the product prominently presents a small monthly installment while failing to give equally prominent notice that the full remaining financed principal may be reported as revolving utilization, and why it refuses to provide a timely remedy after the account has been paid in full and the consumer has documented immediate mortgage-related harm.
